items.title: Jocasta
items.text:
Jocasta keeps an inventory of the devices on your network and logs every change. One binary, with a web UI, a JSON API and an MCP server.

Pre-1.0

A release can change the config format, the database schema or the API with no upgrade path. Pin a version and read the upgrade notes before moving on. The version menu at the top picks the docs for your release.

items.title: How it works
items.text:
1. Sweep the networks you list, every 5 minutes.
  2. File each device under its hardware address. Its IP is a lease.
  3. Log what changed. Add your router, flow exports and DNS resolver for other VLANs, traffic and lookups.

items.title: How a device gets its type
items.text:
After each scan, Jocasta guesses each device's type from:

  • the vendor of its hardware address
  • its name
  • its open TCP ports
  • the DNS-SD services it advertises, and a Google Cast device's model
  • whether it made up its hardware address
  • the name of its network, such as IoT
  • whether it holds the .1 of its subnet
path: How a device gets its type

items.title: Rules
items.text:
Each rule names a type and the facts it needs, such as vendor Brother for a printer, or port 8123 for a Home Assistant hub. The matching rule with the most facts wins. On a tie, the rule listed first wins.

The device page shows the guess as auto with a confidence. High: the rule needed two or more facts, or two rules agree. Low: one weak fact, such as the network's name, and nothing else. Medium: anything between.

When a later scan changes the guess, the change log records Type changed.
path: How a device gets its type

items.title: Set the type yourself
items.text: Open the device, select Edit details, pick a type, and select Save. Scans never change it. The device page still shows the guess. Auto goes back to it.

items.title: Ask why
items.text: The MCP server's explain_device tool returns the facts, the winning rule, and every other rule that matched.

items.title: CLI
items.text:
jocasta <command> [flags]

  serve              Start the web server and the sweep poller.  (default)
  scan <cidr>        Sweep a prefix once and print the result.
  ports [target]     Probe TCP ports on an address, a prefix, or the inventory.
  plugin run <name>  Read one configured source and print what it claims.
  version            Print build information.

  -c, --config       Path to the config file (default "jocasta.yaml")
      --log-level    debug | info | warn | error
      --log-format   text | json

Every command takes --help for its own flags.

items.title: serve
items.text:
jocasta serve                 # host and port from config
jocasta serve -p 9000         # override the port

Starts the HTTP server. When scan.devices.enabled is set, it also starts a poller that sweeps every network in networks on scan.devices.interval. When scan.ports.enabled is set, a second poller port-scans every address the inventory holds on your networks, on scan.ports.interval, and port-scans each new device as soon as a sweep or router read discovers it. Each enabled routeros and openwrt instance is also read for what is plugged into it, on scan.devices.interval. Each enabled netflow instance starts a listener for its router's flow exports, and an hourly prune deletes records older than their retention window, and devices you never curated that no scan has seen within retention.devices.

items.title: scan
items.text:
Runs one sweep and prints a table, or JSON with --json. With --save it also records the sweep in the inventory, under the name from --source, then scan.source, then this host's name.

$ jocasta scan 192.0.2.0/24
IP           MAC                VENDOR   HOSTNAME              RTT     DETAILS
192.0.2.1    00:00:5e:00:53:01  -        gateway.example      1.2ms
192.0.2.10   00:00:5e:00:53:02  -        nas.example          0.8ms
192.0.2.20   00:00:5e:00:53:04  -        -                    3.1ms   self (eth0)

$ jocasta scan 192.0.2.0/24 --save --rate 500 --no-resolve-names

The sweep uses a raw ICMP socket where it can and an unprivileged datagram socket otherwise, so it runs without root. A host with no reverse DNS name is asked for its name over mDNS, then over NetBIOS, then over DNS-SD, then over SSDP, until one gives it a name. --no-resolve-mdns, --no-resolve-netbios, --no-resolve-dnssd and --no-resolve-ssdp turn each off. With --json, each host also lists the services it advertises over DNS-SD.

items.title: ports
items.text:
Probes TCP ports with a plain connect(), so it needs no privileges and cannot change the target. With no argument it scans every current address the inventory holds on your networks: those in networks and the segments a router serves. A neighbour outside them, such as your ISP's gateway, is left alone. Each address is also scanned on the TCP ports its device advertises a service on and the ports recorded open on that device; give an address or a prefix to scan only that. --ports takes a spec like 22,80,443,8000-8100; the default is a curated preset of about a hundred ports a homelab commonly runs. --concurrency caps how many connections are open at once (64 by default). --save records what it finds against the matching devices.

$ jocasta ports 192.0.2.10
ADDRESS      PORT   SERVICE
192.0.2.10   22     ssh
192.0.2.10   443    https

$ jocasta ports --save                      # every known address, recorded
$ jocasta ports 192.0.2.0/24 --ports 1-1024 --json

items.title: plugin run
items.text:
Reads one configured source without starting the server. Use it to check a credential or a firewall rule against the real router. It reads the instance even when it is disabled in config.

$ jocasta plugin run gateway
NETWORK           VLAN  NAME
192.0.2.0/24      -     Trusted
198.51.100.0/24   20    IoT

ADDRESS          MAC                VENDOR  HOSTNAME    STANDING     PRESENT
192.0.2.1        00:00:5e:00:53:01  -       gateway     DHCP_STATIC  true
198.51.100.10    00:00:5e:00:53:09  -       thermostat  DHCP_LEASE   true

$ jocasta plugin run gateway --json --save

After the devices it prints the source's topology: its ports and the VLANs each carries, the hardware addresses learned on each port, and its neighbours. A topology_only instance prints the topology alone. --save records both.

items.title: Devices
items.text:
A device is identified by its hardware (MAC) address. Its IP address is a lease, so your label and notes stay put when the IP changes.

A sweep reads hardware addresses on its own segment only. A device on another segment is known by IP until a router reports its hardware address. The device page says which: by hardware address or by IP address. If a record for that hardware address already exists, the two merge and keep your labels.

Phones, tablets and laptops make up a hardware address per Wi-Fi network. Such an address names no vendor, and each new one is a new device. Devices you never touch are deleted 90 days after they were last seen.

An address the device stops answering on is dropped once the device has answered elsewhere in the same network for 6 hours.

items.title: Networks
items.text: A network is an IP prefix, such as 192.0.2.0/24. Jocasta sweeps the prefixes under networks. A router plugin adds the segments the router serves, with names and VLAN tags.

items.title: Scans
items.text:
A scan is one recorded reading:

  • Sweep. An ICMP echo to every address in networks, then a name lookup for each one that answers. Every 5 minutes.
  • Port scan. A TCP connection to a list of ports on every known address. Off until scan.ports.enabled: true, then every 6 hours. A new device is also scanned as soon as a sweep or router read discovers it.
  • Plugin read. A router's ARP and DHCP tables, read with each sweep. A DNS resolver's query log, read every minute.

The Scans page lists them. To run one by hand, use jocasta scan, jocasta ports or jocasta plugin run.

items.title: Sources
items.text:
Each scan files its facts under a source: sweep:<host> for the sweep, or the plugin's instance name, such as gateway. The device page lists what each source calls the device.

When sources disagree on a name, the higher standing wins. A static DHCP lease beats a name the device announces. See How names are chosen.

items.title: Presence
items.text:
A device is seen recently if a scan saw it in the last 15 minutes, and quiet otherwise. Both come from past scans. Opening a page starts none.

Watched devices log when they go quiet and come back. Others do not: phones and laptops would fill the log. See Get told when a device goes quiet.

items.title: The change log
items.text: The Events page lists every change: new devices, addresses gained and dropped, renames, ports opened and closed, type changes, and your own edits. Notifications send them on.

items.title: What you own
items.text:
Label, group, type, notes, ignored and watched are yours. Scans never write them. See Label, group and ignore devices.

Without a type from you, Jocasta guesses one. See How a device gets its type.

items.title: Retention
items.text:
Record Kept for Setting Change log and scans 90 days retention.history Hourly traffic totals 30 days retention.traffic Hourly DNS lookup counts 30 days retention.dns Devices you never touched, after last seen 90 days retention.devices

0s keeps a record forever.

items.title: Limits
items.text:
• An open port is one that accepted a TCP connection. The service name is a guess from the port number.
  • No recorded ports can mean port scanning is off.
  • Traffic covers only what crossed the router while flow export was on.
  • An internet address is named after the network that announces it. For a cloud address, that is the provider.

items.title: Configure
items.text:
The only setting you need is networks, the prefixes to sweep. Everything else has a default. jocasta.example.yaml lists every setting with its default and a line on what it does, and the configuration reference gives each one's type, allowed values and environment variable.

Settings are read in this order, each overriding the last:

  1. built-in defaults
  2. a YAML file, jocasta.yaml in the working directory, or the path given to --config
  3. environment variables prefixed JOCASTA_

In an environment variable, a double underscore separates levels and a single underscore stays part of the key:

JOCASTA_SCAN__DEVICES__INTERVAL=10m      # scan.devices.interval
JOCASTA_PLUGINS__ROUTEROS__GATEWAY__PASSWORD=change-me

Times are shown in the server's time zone, which in a container is UTC. Name yours to see them in local time. This changes only how times are shown; they are stored in UTC.

location:
  timezone: "Australia/Sydney"   # an IANA zone name

A device you have not labelled, grouped, typed, noted, ignored or watched is deleted once no scan has seen it for 90 days. Phones leave one of these each time they change their privacy address. Anything you set on a device keeps it. Change the window, or set it to 0 to keep every device:

retention:
  devices: "2160h"

Do not commit a jocasta.yaml that holds real addresses or credentials to a repository.

items.title: What to turn on next
items.text:
• Port scanning: set scan.ports.enabled: true to probe every known address on your networks for open TCP ports on a timer. Each address is also probed on the TCP ports its device advertises a service on. See CLI for one-off scans.
  • Routers: devices on every VLAN, and what is plugged in where. See Plugins.
  • Traffic: who each device talks to, from your router's flow exports, with a Traffic page and a live Map. See NetFlow and Tour the web UI.
  • DNS lookups: what each device looks up, from your resolver's query log. See Record what devices look up.
  • Notifications: new devices, opened ports and other changes, sent to ntfy, a signed webhook, or any service that takes an HTTP request. See Notifications.
  • MCP server: lets AI agents query the inventory. See MCP server.
  • JSON API: under /api, for scripts and dashboards. See JSON API.

items.title: Make targets
items.text:
make build          # build to bin/
make test           # go test ./...
make e2e            # browser tests a pull request must pass (needs Chrome)
make e2e-full       # browser tests on every screen and account
make smoke          # read the router, DNS and NetFlow sources in containers (needs Docker)
make lint           # golangci-lint (installs it to bin/ on first run)
make dev            # hot-reload server via air
make gen            # regenerate sqlc models
make new_migration name=<name>
make oui            # rebuild the embedded MAC-vendor table
make htmx           # refresh the vendored htmx
make docs           # build the docs site and check every link (needs uv)
make docs-serve     # preview the docs site at http://localhost:8000

items.title: Browser tests
items.text:
internal/web/e2e drives Chrome over the real server, built with the e2e tag so go test ./... leaves it out. It needs Google Chrome or Chromium on PATH, or E2E_CHROME set to one.

Each page is drawn over four fabricated inventories (empty, a home network, one with extreme data, and one with no accounts), and each dialog, menu and inline edit it opens is drawn too. Every drawing is checked for sideways scrolling, clipped or overlapping text, small tap targets, small text, WCAG 2.2 AA failures (axe-core), script errors and failed requests.

make e2e draws every page as admin on a phone, a tablet and a laptop, in both themes. It takes about two minutes, and CI does not run it: run it before opening a pull request that touches the UI. make e2e-full adds every other screen and account; scripts/release.sh runs it before tagging.

A finding fails the run unless testdata/known.json lists it under an open issue. A fix deletes its entries. make e2e-full also fails on an entry that no longer matches anything.

The run also compares the first screen of every page on the home network with a stored picture in testdata/golden/: on a phone, a tablet and a laptop in light, and the laptop in dark. A picture fails when more than 64 of its pixels changed, which a single word added or lost exceeds. When a change is meant, store the new pictures and commit them with it:

E2E_UPDATE=1 make e2e

To see what changed, set E2E_ARTIFACTS to a directory: each picture that differs is written there beside a map of the changed pixels.

To look at a fixture in a browser:

E2E_SERVE=weird go test -tags e2e -run TestServe -timeout 0 ./internal/web/e2e/

To capture every page and read the findings, with no pass or fail:

E2E_AUDIT=$PWD/tmp/audit TMPDIR=$PWD/tmp go test -tags e2e -run TestAudit -timeout 0 ./internal/web/e2e/

E2E_FIXTURES, E2E_ROLES, E2E_VIEWPORTS, E2E_THEMES and E2E_PAGES narrow either run to a comma-separated list.

items.title: Smoke tests
items.text:
make smoke reads real OpenWrt, RouterOS, Pi-hole, AdGuard Home and Technitium servers and a real NetFlow exporter, each in a container, and checks what jocasta says about them. The plugin tests answer from canned replies; this catches a server that has changed what it sends. It needs Docker and Go, and CI does not run it: run it before opening a pull request that changes one of these plugins or the client under pkg/.

scripts/smoke/smoke.sh up starts the servers on a network of their own, 198.51.100.0/24:

  • OpenWrt is set up as the OpenWrt page describes, with the ACL in docs/openwrt/jocasta.json, and given leases and static hosts.
  • RouterOS CHR runs in QEMU, booted by scripts/smoke/routeros.sh. Its ether1 takes an address over DHCP, as a WAN does, and ether2 sits on the smoke network. It gets a read-only jocasta user, a bridge with an address of its own, a DHCP server with a static lease, a static ARP entry, and Traffic Flow exporting IPFIX, as the RouterOS page sets it up.
  • Pi-hole, AdGuard Home and Technitium each block a name, and AdGuard Home rewrites one. Technitium is set up as the Technitium page describes: a user that can view Logs, its API token, and the Query Logs (Sqlite) app. Pi-hole answers as the other two's upstream, so no lookup leaves the network.
  • pmacct runs in the OpenWrt container's network namespace and exports NetFlow v9 to this host, as the router would.
  • The OpenWrt container sends lookups to each resolver.

Each server's web interface is published on 127.0.0.1, which jocasta reads.

scripts/smoke/smoke.sh check runs jocasta plugin run against each server and checks the rows it prints. It runs TestNetFlowLive in internal/plugin while the OpenWrt container makes a lookup, and again while this host makes a request to the router, and checks the flows each decodes. It also runs the live tests in pkg/openwrt, pkg/routeros and internal/plugin. It writes the config it used to $TMPDIR/jocasta-smoke/jocasta.yaml, so you can point jocasta serve at the same servers. make smoke-down removes them.

Some services need more than Docker. Leave any of them out with SMOKE_SKIP, such as SMOKE_SKIP="technitium netflow" make smoke:

  • routeros: RouterOS runs under QEMU, which emulates the CPU where the host has no KVM. It boots in under a minute either way. Its container joins a second network, which needs Docker 28 or later.
  • technitium: the server downloads the Query Logs app from Technitium's app store, so its container needs internet.
  • netflow: the exporter sends to the network's gateway address, which only Docker on Linux puts on the host.

To change a setting, set the matching variable:

  • SMOKE_REGISTRY pulls the images from a mirror, such as mirror.gcr.io, when Docker Hub limits your pulls.
  • SMOKE_PIHOLE_IMAGE, SMOKE_ADGUARD_IMAGE, SMOKE_OPENWRT_IMAGE, SMOKE_ROUTEROS_IMAGE, SMOKE_TECHNITIUM_IMAGE and SMOKE_PMACCT_IMAGE test another release. MikroTik publishes no image; the RouterOS one is evilfreelancer/docker-routeros, which carries the CHR disk and QEMU.
  • SMOKE_PIHOLE_PORT, SMOKE_ADGUARD_PORT, SMOKE_ADGUARD_SETUP_PORT, SMOKE_OPENWRT_PORT, SMOKE_TECHNITIUM_PORT and SMOKE_ROUTEROS_PORT move the published ports, 18081 to 18086 by default. SMOKE_FLOW_PORT and SMOKE_ROUTEROS_FLOW_PORT move the ports the NetFlow and IPFIX exports arrive on, 2055 and 2056 by default.

netifd cannot create the br-lan bridge inside a container, so the OpenWrt container's lan sits on eth0. Its bridge table and VLANs are empty, and the unit tests cover reading them.

items.title: Docs
items.text:
The pages in docs/ are published with Zensical to GitHub Pages, one version for each minor release and one for main. The Docs workflow builds every pull request that touches them with make docs, which fails on a broken link or anchor. A merge to main publishes the dev version, and a v* tag publishes that minor version as latest. Both are pushed to the gh-pages branch with the Zensical fork of mike.

When you change the docs:

  • Add a new page to nav in mkdocs.yml, and to the llmstxt sections there, or the site leaves it out of the sidebar and llms.txt.
  • A new plugin gets a page under docs/plugins/ and a line in the table on the plugins overview. A DNS resolver also gets a column on Record what devices look up.
  • A new setting gets a row in the configuration reference. TestReferenceDocumentsEveryKey fails until it has one, and fails on a row for a setting that no longer exists.
  • Keep docs/setup.md and docs/mcp.md. Earlier releases link to their sections on GitHub, and each section there points to where it moved.

items.title: Release
items.text:
After CI passes on main, run the following. It runs make e2e-full first, so Chrome must be installed.

./scripts/release.sh v0.10.0

The script requires a clean working tree and a local main that matches origin/main. It checks that the tag is unused, creates an annotated tag, and pushes it to trigger the release workflow. It does not wait for the build.

The GitHub release and the changelog page are written from the commit messages, as cliff.toml sets out. To give a minor release highlights, merge docs/releases/<major.minor>.md before tagging its .0.

items.title: Layout
items.text:
• cmd/jocasta: CLI entry point.
  • internal/scanner: the ICMP sweep, and the reverse DNS, mDNS, NetBIOS, DNS-SD and SSDP lookups that name what answers.
  • internal/plugin: sources beyond the sweep (RouterOS, OpenWrt, NetFlow, Technitium, Pi-hole, AdGuard Home).
  • internal/inventory: the store, covering identity resolution, address handling, device classification and the change log.
  • internal/classify: the rules that guess a device's type from its vendor, name and open ports.
  • internal/notify: sends each finished scan's changes to ntfy, a webhook or a templated HTTP request.
  • internal/web, internal/api: the HTML UI and the JSON API.
  • internal/db: connection, migrations, generated queries.

Queries are SQLC-generated from internal/db/queries/. The schema is in internal/db/migrations/.

items.title: Add a notification service
items.text:
Most services take an HTTP request, and the http provider reaches them with a body template and no new code. For one of those, add a recipe to Send to another service. TestRecipesInTheDocsRender renders every recipe there, so a broken one fails the tests.

A service gets a provider of its own only when the http provider cannot reach it: it needs more than one request, a protocol other than HTTP, or signing a template cannot do. Each provider is in internal/notify, in a file of its own, as ntfy.go and webhook.go are:

  1. Add a struct with koanf tags for its settings, and give it Validate, Host and Send. Send must not put a credential in its error. post covers a service that takes an HTTP request.
  2. Add a field for it to notify.Config, and a line to Config.provider.
  3. Add an example to jocasta.example.yaml, and a row for each setting to the configuration reference.

The notifier, the settings page, the store and cmd need no change.

items.title: Add a name source
items.text:
Each name carries a standing, dbtype.HostnameSource, which says how it was learned. When sources disagree, the name with the higher standing is shown.

  1. Add a constant for it in internal/db/dbtype/enum.go and add it to hostnameSources.
  2. Give it a place in HostnameSource.Rank, and say why in the comment there. A name that resolves ranks above one a device only claims.
  3. Word it for the device page in standing, in internal/web/funcs.go.
  4. List it in Name devices.

A sweep that asks devices for their names takes two more steps:

  1. Add its lookup in internal/scanner, in a file of its own, and ask it in enrich in rank order. A query sent to each host is a nameProtocol, as in mdns.go and netbios.go. Any other lookup is a nameLookup, as askSSDP in ssdp.go is, or names hosts itself, as browseServices does with dnssd.go.
  2. Add it to HostnameSource.Swept, so a lower-ranked lookup never replaces its name on the sweep's claim.

The column has no CHECK, so a new standing needs no migration.

items.title: Screenshots
items.text: The images in docs/ui.md are taken against a database of fabricated devices, never real network data: addresses from RFC 5737, hardware addresses from RFC 7042, invented names. Internet peers are well-known public services, so their organisations and countries resolve.

items.title: Label, group and ignore devices
items.text:
These fields are yours. Scans never write them, and they stay with the device when its address or name changes. Editing needs an Admin or Editor account.

  • Label: the name shown everywhere. Up to 200 characters.
  • Group: files devices together, such as Office. The device list filters by it. Up to 100 characters.
  • Type: sets the icon. Auto keeps Jocasta's guess; see How a device gets its type.
  • Notes: free text. Up to 2,000 characters.
  • Ignored: hides the device from lists and counts.
  • Watched: logs when it goes quiet or comes back; see Get told when a device goes quiet.

items.title: Edit a device
items.text:
1. In Devices, select the device.
  2. Select Edit details, change the fields, and select Save.

An empty field is cleared. Each edit goes in the change log.

To change only the label and group, select the pencil at the end of the row in the device list.

items.title: Ignore a device
items.text:
For a device you know and never want to see, such as a neighbour's printer: in Edit details, tick Ignore this device and select Save.

The sweep still records it. The port scan skips it, and notifications leave it out. Show ignored in the device list filters brings it back into view.

items.title: From a script or an agent
items.text: PATCH /api/devices/{id} in the JSON API, or the update_device_curation tool in the MCP server. Both need a read_write token. The MCP prompt triage_devices proposes a label, group and type for each device that has none.

items.title: Install
items.text: For a guided first run, see Your first inventory.

items.title: Container image
items.text:
Images for amd64 and arm64 are on the GitHub Container Registry, tagged latest and per release, such as :v0.11.1. The image is distroless and runs as non-root. It listens on 0.0.0.0:8080, keeps its database in /data, and reads /data/jocasta.yaml.

docker runCompose 
docker run -d --name jocasta --network host \
  -v jocasta-data:/data \
  -v ./jocasta.yaml:/data/jocasta.yaml:ro \
  ghcr.io/pushkar-anand/jocasta:latest

services:
  jocasta:
    image: ghcr.io/pushkar-anand/jocasta:latest
    network_mode: host
    restart: unless-stopped
    volumes:
      - jocasta-data:/data
      - ./jocasta.yaml:/data/jocasta.yaml:ro

volumes:
  jocasta-data:

Use host networking. On a bridge network (-p 8080:8080) the sweep finds hosts but no hardware addresses, and mDNS, DNS-SD and SSDP names never arrive. A router plugin fills the first gap. Neither mode needs extra capabilities.

items.title: Prebuilt binaries
items.text:
Archives for Linux, macOS and Windows, on amd64 and arm64, are on the releases page, with a checksums.txt.

  1. Extract jocasta from the archive for your system.
  2. Put a jocasta.yaml next to it.
  3. From that directory, run jocasta serve. No root needed.

It listens on localhost:8080. Set server.host: 0.0.0.0 to reach it from other machines.

items.title: From source
items.text:
Needs Go 1.27 or newer.

git clone https://github.com/pushkar-anand/jocasta.git
cd jocasta
make build            # -> bin/jocasta
make docker           # -> jocasta:latest

items.title: First run
items.text:
The first visit asks for the admin account. Until it exists, anyone who reaches the page can create it, so do it straight away. More users: Manage users and sign-in.

Over plain HTTP, sign-in needs server.auth.cookie_secure: false; see Serve over HTTPS.

Migrations run at startup. Before upgrading, see Back up and upgrade.

items.title: How names are chosen
items.text:
A device can be named by more than one source. The name shown is the one from the source ranked highest here. A label you give a device is shown in place of all of them; see Label, group and ignore devices.

  1. Reverse DNS, looked up for each address a sweep finds.
  2. A static DHCP lease on your router.
  3. mDNS, asked of each address the sweep finds that has no reverse DNS name.
  4. A dynamic DHCP lease on your router.
  5. NetBIOS, asked of each address the sweep finds that has no name from reverse DNS or mDNS.
  6. DNS-SD, the name each address still without a name gives the services it advertises.
  7. SSDP, the label in the UPnP description of each address still without a name.

When two names of the same rank disagree, the device keeps the one it has while any source still gives it, and otherwise takes the one heard from last. A device holding several addresses, such as a router with an address on each VLAN, gets a name from each, and keeps one rather than taking whichever address was read last. The device page lists the name each source gives for each address. Reverse DNS names that systemd-resolved makes up, such as _gateway, are not used. Once a sweep has a name for a device, a lower-ranked lookup does not replace it. The device keeps that name until the lookup that gave it, or a higher-ranked one, answers with another.

items.title: mDNS
items.text:
mDNS gives a name to phones, TVs, printers and computers that reverse DNS does not know, such as living-room-tv.local. Jocasta sends one query to each such device, on UDP port 5353, and needs no host networking or multicast for it. Most devices answer only a query from their own segment, as the mDNS standard asks, so devices on other segments rarely get an mDNS name.

To turn it off, set scan.devices.resolve_mdns: false. It does not depend on scan.devices.resolve_names: with reverse DNS off, no device has a reverse DNS name, so every device that answers the sweep is asked over mDNS.

items.title: NetBIOS
items.text: NetBIOS gives a name to Windows computers and to devices running Samba, such as a NAS. A NetBIOS name, such as DESKTOP-4F2K, is 15 characters at most. Jocasta sends one query to each device still without a name, on UDP port 137. Windows answers only with file and printer sharing turned on, and by default only a query from its own segment. To turn it off, set scan.devices.resolve_netbios: false.

items.title: DNS-SD
items.text:
DNS-SD names TVs, speakers, printers and other devices that advertise their services over mDNS but do not answer an mDNS query for their own name. After each sweep, Jocasta asks the multicast group 224.0.0.251:5353 which service types are on the segment, then which devices offer each one. A Google Cast device is named after the name its owner gave it in the Home app, such as Living Room TV. Any other device is named after the name most of its services share, leaving out names that are only a serial number or other ID. Jocasta binds UDP port 5353 to hear the answers, sharing it with any mDNS responder on the same machine, such as Avahi. Like SSDP, it reaches only Jocasta's own segment, and only with host networking. To turn it off, set scan.devices.resolve_dnssd: false.

Jocasta also records the services each device advertises, named or not, and lists the ones the latest sweep heard in the device page's Ports table. The port scan probes each advertised TCP port, so the table says whether it answers. The scan also probes every port recorded open, so when a service moves to a new port, its old port closes. A port probed only because a device advertised it opens and closes without an event, since a phone advertises on a new random port each time. The classifier reads every service heard within retention.history, so one sweep missing an answer does not change a device's type: a print service marks a printer, and the Android TV remote service a TV. A service no sweep has heard within retention.history is deleted.

items.title: SSDP
items.text: SSDP names TVs, speakers, media players, printers and routers that nothing else names. The name is the label the device shows its owner, such as Living Room TV. After a sweep that leaves a device without a name, Jocasta sends one SSDP search to the multicast group 239.255.255.250:1900. For each device still without a name that answers, it fetches the UPnP description the answer points to and takes the friendlyName from it. It fetches only from the address that answered, over plain HTTP, at most 64 KB and for at most 2 seconds. The search reaches only Jocasta's own segment, and only with host networking, since a bridge network does not pass multicast. To turn it off, set scan.devices.resolve_ssdp: false.

items.title: Your first inventory
items.text:
Run Jocasta in a container, sweep your network, name a device, and get a message on your phone when it goes quiet. About 10 minutes.

You need a Linux machine on the network with Docker, and the network's prefix. ip -4 addr shows it: inet 192.0.2.20/24 means 192.0.2.0/24.

items.title: 1. Write the config
items.text:
Create jocasta.yaml in an empty directory:

networks:
  - "192.0.2.0/24"

server:
  auth:
    cookie_secure: false   # sign in over plain HTTP

items.title: 2. Start Jocasta
items.text:
docker run -d --name jocasta --network host \
  -v jocasta-data:/data \
  -v ./jocasta.yaml:/data/jocasta.yaml:ro \
  ghcr.io/pushkar-anand/jocasta:latest

Host networking lets the sweep read hardware addresses.

items.title: 3. Create the admin account
items.text:
Open http://<host>:8080. Enter a username and a password of 8 or more characters, and select Create admin account.

Until this account exists, anyone who reaches the page can create it.

items.title: 4. Look at the first sweep
items.text:
The first sweep runs at startup. Open Devices: one row per device, with its addresses, vendor and name.

Rows with no vendor are usually phones and laptops, which make up their hardware address. Rows with no name belong to devices that did not answer a name lookup.

items.title: 5. Name a device
items.text:
1. Select a device you recognise.
  2. Select Edit details.
  3. Set Label to Office printer and Group to Office.
  4. Select Save.

The device list shows the new label.

items.title: 6. Watch it
items.text:
On the device's page, select Watch.

A watched device goes quiet 15 minutes after the last scan that saw it. To try it, turn the device off for 20 minutes and open Events.

items.title: 7. Get a message on your phone
items.text:
1. Install ntfy on your phone and subscribe to a topic. Topics are public, so pick a name nobody would guess, such as jocasta-k3v9q2.

  2. Add it to jocasta.yaml:

    notify:
  phone:
    ntfy:
      url: "https://ntfy.sh/jocasta-k3v9q2"

  3. Restart: docker restart jocasta.

  4. Open the account menu, top right, and select Notifications.
  5. Under phone, tick Watched device went quiet and Watched device came back. Select Save.
  6. Select Send test. "Jocasta test" arrives on your phone.

items.title: Tour the web UI
items.text:
This page walks through each page of the web UI. They read the same data as the JSON API, and the Overview, Map and Topology refresh themselves.

The screenshots below use synthetic data: addresses from RFC 5737, hardware addresses from RFC 7042, invented names. The internet peers are well-known public services, so their organisations resolve.

items.title: Overview
items.text: Per-network counts, a presence summary, the last sweep, and recent changes.

items.title: Device list
items.text: Filter by group, network or presence. Search by name, address or vendor. Ignored devices are hidden unless you ask for them.

items.title: Device page
items.text:
Everything Jocasta knows about one device:

  • Identity: what Jocasta resolved the device to be, and whether it is known by its hardware address or only its IP.
  • What you call it: label, group, type and notes. No scan or plugin writes these.
  • Connected: the path from the internet to the device, through each router, switch and access point, with the port or Wi-Fi network, band and VLAN at each step. A device plugged straight into a read port shows the link's rate, and a Wi-Fi client its rate each way and its signal. When a wired link runs below what both ends can, the page says so. Show on topology opens the Topology page on the device.
  • Addresses: every address the device has held, and the network each is on.
  • Ports: once a port scan has reached the device (see CLI), the TCP ports it listens on, and the ones it has since closed.
  • Sources: what each source, such as the sweep or the router, calls the device at each address it reported, and when it last heard from it.
  • History: the device's entries in the change log.

items.title: Talks to
items.text:
When traffic collection is set up (see NetFlow), this section shows who the device exchanged data with over the last 24 hours, 7 days or 30 days.

The top of the section shows data received and sent, how many peers on your network, and how many organisations on the internet. Below that is one tab per network segment and one for the internet, each with a count. The busiest tab opens first.

On a segment's tab, each peer is one row, whatever services it was reached on, and links to its page when it is a device. Addresses no device holds collapse into one row per subnet. The Internet tab groups addresses by the organisation that announces them. The search box and the filters narrow the section to one service, or by name, address or organisation.

Each row shows who opened its connections: "→ 12" means the device opened 12, "← 3" means the peer opened 3. A row can show both. The direction filter keeps one side only.

When something on the internet tried the device without exchanging any data, such as a knock on a forwarded port, a note says how many addresses tried, from how many organisations, and on which ports. Tries on the router's outside address are counted under the router. Jocasta learns that address from the flows themselves.

Connections the device started that carried no data (a refused port, one nobody answered, a ping) are counted at the top and left out of the tabs. Tick "Show tries with no data" to add each to the row of the peer it went to, with how many got an answer and the ports tried. When they add up to probing the network, a notice at the top says so.

The Broadcasts tab lists packets the device sent to a whole subnet or multicast group. These are mostly discovery protocols, such as mDNS, SSDP, DHCP or a sync tool finding its peers. Names are guessed from the port and group.

items.title: Traffic page
items.text:
When traffic collection is set up, this page summarises the whole network over the last 24 hours, 7 days or 30 days. Its cards:

  • Probing your network: devices that, within an hour, tried 20 or more addresses, or 20 or more ports on one address, without exchanging any data. A device you run scans from shows up here too.
  • Reached from the internet: each device and service that someone on the internet connected to. A service on the same port at both ends, such as a VPN server on IKE, is left out, since its clients look like replies.
  • Probed from the internet: connections from the internet that carried no data, per device and on the router's outside address.
  • Busiest devices and Top internet destinations. Each organisation opens to the devices behind it.
  • New this week: organisations a device first exchanged data with in the last 7 days.

A tab per network segment narrows every card to that segment's devices, with its totals at the top. You can also narrow the page to one group.

If the router's outside address is itself private, because the ISP's carrier-grade NAT or another router sits in front of it, the page says so. Nothing on the internet can connect in over IPv4 then, so the two internet cards stay empty.

items.title: Map
items.text:
When traffic collection is set up, the Map draws the last hour's traffic as a tree. It redraws every minute, which is how often new traffic is recorded.

  • The router sits in the middle, with a hub for each network and one for the internet.
  • Devices and organisations fan out around their hub. The busiest 60 devices and 12 organisations are drawn.
  • A branch is thicker the more traffic passed along it, and moves when anything under it was active in the last 15 minutes.
  • A faint line joins each device to what it exchanged traffic with: an organisation, or a device on another network. Traffic between two devices on the same network never passes the router, so it is not drawn.
  • The legend in the top right names each network's colour with its device count. Point at one to pick out its devices.

Click a device or organisation to light up its lines, name the services on each ("https", "mqtts", "port 123 UDP") and dim everything else. Click the device again to open its page. Click the empty map or press Escape to go back.

Scroll or pinch to zoom, drag to pan, and double-click to zoom in on a spot. The search box dims everything that does not match, and Enter zooms to the first match. The view, the search and each device's place are kept across redraws.

items.title: World
items.text:
The World tab puts the same hour's internet traffic on a map of the world.

  • A country is shaded darker the more traffic went to addresses registered there. A marker pulses on the ones active in the last 15 minutes.
  • A line runs from your network's country to each of the others, thicker the more it carried and moving while active.
  • Click a country for the devices and organisations behind its traffic. The search finds countries by name.

Your network's country comes from the router's outside address, or from location.country when that address is private (see NetFlow).

A country is where an address is registered. For a big provider that is often its home country, and the server itself may be elsewhere.

items.title: Topology
items.text:
The Topology page draws the network from the internet down (see Show what is plugged in where). It redraws every minute.

  • The internet sits at the top, the router below it, and each switch and access point hangs from the port it is plugged into. A thick line is a trunk, a thin one carries one VLAN, and a dashed one is Wi-Fi.
  • Under each box, its wired devices are grouped by VLAN, with each device's port on the right. Its Wi-Fi devices are grouped by network, with each device's band.
  • A solid box is a device Jocasta reads. A dashed box only announced itself to one it reads. A dotted box is inferred from several devices sharing one port behind it. When one of them is a hypervisor, the box is that device and the rest are its virtual machines. To mark a host Jocasta has not recognised, set its type to Hypervisor on its page. A dotted box whose devices mostly have a virtual machine's hardware address is labelled Hypervisor.
  • A device that has gone quiet stays where it was last seen, dimmed. Devices seen recently that no router, switch or access point has seen on a port are listed under the tree.
  • The legend in the top right names each VLAN's colour with its device count. Point at one to pick out its devices.

Click a device to light the path from the internet down to it, and click it again to open its page. Search, zoom and pan work as on the Map.

items.title: Network page
items.text: One segment, its VLAN tag and name, and the devices on it.

items.title: Events
items.text: The full change log.

items.title: Light theme
items.text: A toggle in the header switches themes; the choice is stored per browser.

items.title: JSON API
items.text: Jocasta serves its inventory as JSON under /api, for scripts and dashboards. It takes the same API tokens as the MCP server.

items.title: Authenticate
items.text:
Create an API token and send it with each request:

curl -H "Authorization: Bearer <token>" http://<host>:8080/api/devices

A read token can make GET requests only. A read_write token can also change devices. A token never expires unless you chose 30 days, 90 days or 1 year when you created it. An expired token is refused like a revoked one, and stays listed until you revoke it.

GET /api/livez answers without a token, for health checks.

items.title: Endpoints
items.text:
Request Returns GET /api/livez Whether the server is up. GET /api/stats Counts across the inventory. GET /api/groups The device groups in use. GET /api/devices The device list. GET /api/devices/{id} One device. PATCH /api/devices/{id} Changes a device's label, group, type, notes or ignored flag. Needs a read_write token. PATCH /api/devices/{id}/watch Starts or stops watching a device. Needs a read_write token. GET /api/devices/{id}/events A device's change log. GET /api/devices/{id}/traffic Who a device talked to. Needs traffic recorded. GET /api/devices/{id}/dns What a device looked up. Needs lookups recorded. GET /api/events The change log across all devices. GET /api/scans Past scans.

An error comes back as an RFC 9457 problem document, with a title and a detail saying what to change.

items.title: Browser access
items.text: A page on another origin can read /api only when its origin is listed in server.cors.allowed_origins. See the configuration reference.

items.title: MCP server
items.text:
Jocasta can serve the inventory to AI agents such as Claude Code over the Model Context Protocol. It is off by default.

An agent connected this way can answer questions such as:

  • What joined the network this week?
  • Which devices have SSH open?
  • What is 192.0.2.47, and when was it first seen?
  • Which devices talked to a new organisation today?

With a read_write token it can also label and group devices. It reads what past scans recorded and never starts a scan.

items.title: Turn it on
items.text:
1. Set server.mcp.enabled: true in the config file, or JOCASTA_SERVER__MCP__ENABLED=true. While it is off, /mcp answers 404.
  2. Create an API token; see API tokens. A read token is offered only the tools that read the inventory. A read_write token is also offered the tools that change it.

The endpoint is /mcp, using the Streamable HTTP transport, with the token sent as Authorization: Bearer <token>. Clients discover the available tools and prompts when they connect.

Device hostnames and vendor names are reported by the devices themselves, so anything on your network can choose what an agent reads there. Give an agent a read token unless it needs to change something.

items.title: Connect a client
items.text:
The examples use https://jocasta.example.test/mcp; replace it with your server's address.

Claude Code

claude mcp add --transport http jocasta https://jocasta.example.test/mcp \
  --header "Authorization: Bearer <token>"

Codex

Codex reads the token from an environment variable, which keeps it out of its config file:

export JOCASTA_TOKEN=<token>
codex mcp add jocasta --url https://jocasta.example.test/mcp \
  --bearer-token-env-var JOCASTA_TOKEN

Hermes Agent

Put JOCASTA_TOKEN=<token> in ~/.hermes/.env, add the server to ~/.hermes/config.yaml, then run /reload-mcp in a running session:

mcp_servers:
  jocasta:
    url: "https://jocasta.example.test/mcp"
    headers:
      Authorization: "Bearer ${JOCASTA_TOKEN}"

Other clients

Any client that supports Streamable HTTP and lets you set a request header works. For clients that can only launch a local server over stdio, a bridge such as mcp-remote can forward to the endpoint.

items.title: Tools
items.text: Tool What it answers list_devices Which devices match a search, group, network, type, presence (seen recently or quiet) or whether you watch them. get_device Everything about one device: addresses, ports, advertised services, sources, your labels, and where it is plugged in and how fast. explain_device Why a device has the class it has: the facts the classifier used, the rule that decided and every other rule that matched. list_events What changed, across the network or for one device. list_networks, get_network The network segments, and how many devices are on each. list_groups The groups you filed devices under. get_stats How many devices were seen recently, are quiet, are ignored or were discovered in the last 24 hours. get_port_overview Open ports across the network, and the commonest services. list_scans When scans ran, and what they found. list_traffic Who devices exchanged data with. Needs traffic collection. list_dns The names a device looked up, and which were blocked. Needs lookups recorded. get_topology What is plugged in where, and how fast each link runs. Needs topology set up. update_device_curation Sets a device's label, group, type, notes and ignored flag. read_write tokens only. watch_device Watches a device, or stops, so you are told when it goes quiet or comes back. read_write tokens only.

items.title: Prompts
items.text:
Prompts are saved procedures you start yourself; the agent then carries them out with the tools. In Claude Code they appear as slash commands, such as /mcp__jocasta__weekly_report.

Prompt What it does triage_devices Finds the devices that need attention: unlabelled, doubtfully classified, or likely duplicates left by a randomised hardware address. Proposes a label, group and type for each. With a read_write token the agent applies the proposals you confirm; with a read token it only proposes. weekly_report Summarises what changed over the last 7 days: new devices, devices gone quiet, organisations a device reached for the first time (when traffic collection is set up), port changes, identity changes, and what may need a look. Takes an optional days argument, from 1 to 90. It can reach back only as far as retention.history keeps the change log.

items.title: Errors
items.text: Errors are RFC 9457 problem documents, as in the HTTP API. A failed tool call returns one as the text of an error result, with the tool name as instance. The cause of a 500 stays in the server log.

items.title: Notifications
items.text:
Jocasta can send what each scan changed to an ntfy topic, as a signed JSON POST to a URL of your own, or to any service that takes an HTTP request, such as Discord, Slack or Telegram. See Send to another service.

  1. Under notify in the config file, add each destination by name, with one service block:
notify:
  phone:
    ntfy:
      url: "https://ntfy.example.com/jocasta"   # the topic's address, as ntfy shows it
      token: ""                                 # or JOCASTA_NOTIFY__PHONE__NTFY__TOKEN
  automation:
    webhook:
      url: "https://hooks.example.com/jocasta"
      secret: "change-me"                       # required; signs each request

A destination is on unless it says enabled: false. 2. Restart Jocasta so it reads the change. 3. Open the account menu at the top right, and select Notifications. 4. For each destination, tick the kinds of change it is sent, then select Save. 5. Optional: select Send test. A message titled "Jocasta test" arrives at the destination.

Each scan that changes something is sent as one message, such as "2 new devices on 192.0.2.0/24". The first scan of a network, when every device it finds is new, is sent as a count ("Found 42 devices"). Changes to devices you ignore, and your own edits, are left out. A message that cannot be delivered is logged and shown on the Notifications page, and is not sent again.

Every notify setting, with its default and allowed values, is in the configuration reference.

items.title: Send to another service
items.text:
The http service posts each message with a body you write as a template, so it reaches any service that takes an HTTP request. Copy the recipe for yours below, under notify.

The template is a Go template. It is given:

  • .Title and .Body: the message's title, such as "2 new devices on 192.0.2.0/24", and its text, one change per line.
  • .ScanID: the scan the changes came from, 0 for a test.
  • .Events: each change, with .Kind, .DeviceID, .Device and .Change.
  • json: writes a value as JSON, quoted and escaped. Write every value in a JSON body with it, as {{ json .Title }}: device names can hold quotes and the body holds line breaks.
  • truncate: cuts a string to a number of characters and ends it with …, as {{ .Body | truncate 2000 | json }}. A message lists up to 20 changes, and long device names can take it past a service's limit, which the service answers with an error.

The body is sent as application/json unless headers names another Content-Type. Jocasta renders the template with two sample messages when it starts: one with a change, and the test message, which has none. If the template does not parse, or its output does not parse as JSON, Jocasta reports it and does not start.

A device names itself, so its name can hold text a chat service reads as a mention, such as @everyone, or as formatting. The Slack, Telegram, Gotify, Pushover and Apprise recipes send plain text. Discord has no plain-text mode, so its recipe turns mentions off and a device name can still show formatted.

Discord, with the channel's webhook URL from its Integrations settings:

discord:
  http:
    url: "https://discord.com/api/webhooks/<id>/<token>"
    body: '{"content": {{ printf "%s\n%s" .Title .Body | truncate 2000 | json }}, "allowed_mentions": {"parse": []}}'

Slack, with an incoming webhook URL. The message goes in a plain_text block, which Slack shows as written. The title is also sent as text, which Slack shows in its notifications:

slack:
  http:
    url: "https://hooks.slack.com/services/<path>"
    body: '{"text": {{ json .Title }}, "blocks": [{"type": "section", "text": {"type": "plain_text", "text": {{ printf "%s\n%s" .Title .Body | truncate 3000 | json }}}}]}'

Telegram, with a bot's token and the chat to post in:

telegram:
  http:
    url: "https://api.telegram.org/bot<token>/sendMessage"
    body: '{"chat_id": "<chat id>", "text": {{ printf "%s\n%s" .Title .Body | truncate 4096 | json }}}'

Gotify, with an application's token:

gotify:
  http:
    url: "https://gotify.example.com/message"
    headers:
      X-Gotify-Key: "<app token>"
    body: '{"title": {{ json .Title }}, "message": {{ json .Body }}, "priority": 5}'

Pushover, with an application's token and your user key:

pushover:
  http:
    url: "https://api.pushover.net/1/messages.json"
    body: '{"token": "<app token>", "user": "<user key>", "title": {{ json .Title }}, "message": {{ .Body | truncate 1024 | json }}}'

For email, SMS, Microsoft Teams, Signal and many more, run an Apprise API server beside Jocasta. Save the services' Apprise URLs under a key in Apprise, then post to that key:

apprise:
  http:
    url: "http://apprise.example.com:8000/notify/jocasta"
    body: '{"title": {{ json .Title }}, "body": {{ json .Body }}}'

Home Assistant, n8n and Node-RED take any JSON, so they use the webhook service. For Home Assistant, add an automation with a webhook trigger and point a webhook destination at it. Home Assistant does not check the signature, but a secret is still required. The automation reads the message as trigger.json.title and trigger.json.message, and each change under trigger.json.events.

home_assistant:
  webhook:
    url: "http://homeassistant.local:8123/api/webhook/<webhook id>"
    secret: "change-me"

items.title: Get told when a device goes quiet
items.text:
Watch the devices whose absence you would want to hear about, such as a server, a NAS or a camera. A watched device goes quiet when no scan has seen it for longer than the online window, 15 minutes by default, and comes back when one sees it again. Phones and laptops do both all day, so devices you do not watch never log either.

  1. On the device's page, select Watch.
  2. Open the account menu at the top right, and select Notifications.
  3. For a destination, tick Watched device went quiet and Watched device came back, then select Save.

A message reads "1 device went quiet on 192.0.2.0/24", with a line such as "NAS went quiet after 18 minutes without an answer". The change log records both kinds whether or not a destination is sent them. To list the watched devices that are down now, filter the device list to Watched only and Quiet.

Only a scan that could have seen a device decides it went quiet: a sweep of a network it has an address on, or a read of a router that lists it. A device on a network nothing scans stays as it was last seen. A router read that fails part way decides nothing.

To change how long a device may go unseen, set the online window. It also decides what the device list counts as seen recently:

inventory:
  online_window: "30m"
path: Get told when a device goes quiet

items.title: Check a webhook's signature
items.text:
A webhook request is a POST whose JSON body has title, message, scan_id and events. Two headers come with it:

  • X-Jocasta-Signature-256: sha256= and the hex HMAC-SHA256 of the raw body, keyed with the destination's secret.
  • X-Jocasta-Delivery: a random id for this request. Log it, and drop a delivery you have already handled.

To check a request, compute the HMAC over the body exactly as received, before parsing it, and compare it with the header in constant time. In Go:

mac := hmac.New(sha256.New, []byte(secret))
mac.Write(body)
want := "sha256=" + hex.EncodeToString(mac.Sum(nil))
ok := hmac.Equal([]byte(want), []byte(r.Header.Get("X-Jocasta-Signature-256")))

Reject the request when ok is false.

items.title: Back up and upgrade
items.text: Everything lives in one SQLite database: inventory, change log, traffic, accounts, tokens and notification choices. Keep it and your config file.

items.title: Back up
items.text:
The database is /data/jocasta.db in the container. Recent writes can sit in jocasta.db-wal beside it, so stop Jocasta and copy the whole directory:

docker stop jocasta
docker run --rm -v jocasta-data:/data -v "$PWD":/backup alpine \
  cp -a /data /backup/jocasta-backup
docker start jocasta

The copy holds password hashes and two-factor secrets.

To restore, stop Jocasta, put the files back, and start it.

items.title: Upgrade
items.text:
Jocasta is pre-1.0. A release can change the config format or the schema with no upgrade path.

  1. Read the upgrade notes for every release after yours.
  2. Back up.
  3. Pull the new tag, such as :v0.11.1, and recreate the container.

The schema updates at startup.

items.title: Downgrade
items.text: Restore the backup from before the upgrade. An older release started on a newer database migrates the schema down and drops the newer data.

items.title: Serve over HTTPS
items.text:
Jocasta speaks plain HTTP. Put a reverse proxy with a certificate in front of it.

The session cookie is HTTPS-only by default, so plain HTTP sign-in from any address but localhost needs server.auth.cookie_secure: false. Remove it once the proxy is up.

items.title: Caddy
items.text:
Caddy fetches and renews the certificate. On the same machine:

jocasta.example.com {
    reverse_proxy localhost:8080
}

For a name only your network resolves, add tls internal. Caddy then signs the certificate itself, and each browser has to trust it once.

items.title: Other proxies
items.text: Pass the Host header through unchanged. Jocasta checks it against Origin to refuse cross-site form posts from browsers that send no Sec-Fetch-Site. In nginx: proxy_set_header Host $host;.

items.title: Name the proxy
items.text:
Sign-in attempts are limited per client address. Behind a proxy every request comes from the proxy's address, so all clients share one allowance until Jocasta knows to read the client from X-Forwarded-For:

server:
  trusted_proxies:
    - "127.0.0.1"

List each proxy's address or range. Caddy, nginx and Traefik set the header.

items.title: Close the plain port
items.text:
With the proxy on the same machine, listen on loopback only:

server:
  host: "127.0.0.1"

The container image sets JOCASTA_SERVER__HOST=0.0.0.0, which wins over the file. Pass -e JOCASTA_SERVER__HOST=127.0.0.1 to docker run instead.

items.title: Fix common problems
items.text: Not listed here? Ask in GitHub issues with the log lines around the problem.

items.title: Devices have no hardware address or vendor
items.text:
On a bridge network, the container reads its own neighbour table, which holds none of your devices. Use --network host.

Devices on other segments need a router plugin.

items.title: One phone shows up as several devices
items.text: It makes up a new hardware address now and then, and each one is a new device. Untouched ones are deleted after 90 days. On your own phone, turn off the private address for your home Wi-Fi.

items.title: A device is missing
items.text: The sweep finds devices that answer ping. Windows drops ping by default. A router plugin lists such devices from the router's tables.

items.title: "no usable ICMP socket"
items.text:
A binary run without root needs unprivileged ICMP for its group:

sysctl net.ipv4.ping_group_range

Widen the range to cover Jocasta's group, or use the container image.

items.title: No mDNS, DNS-SD or SSDP names
items.text: These reach Jocasta's own segment only, and DNS-SD and SSDP need multicast. Use --network host. See How names are chosen.

items.title: The sign-in page keeps coming back
items.text: The session cookie is HTTPS-only. See Serve over HTTPS.

items.title: A form shows "Cross-origin request refused"
items.text: Your reverse proxy changes the Host header. See Serve over HTTPS.

items.title: A plugin reads as "source rejected credentials"
items.text:
Test it alone: jocasta plugin run gateway.

  • RouterOS: the user needs read access, and the www-ssl service on, or www with ssl: false.
  • OpenWrt: the login needs the ACL file.
  • Technitium: the token's user needs View on Logs.
  • An environment variable beats the file. Check both.

items.title: The Traffic page stays empty
items.text:
• exporters must list the address the exports come from. The log warns "dropping datagrams from a sender not listed in exporters" with that address.
  • On a bridge network, publish the port as UDP: -p 2055:2055/udp.
  • Open the listen port in the host's firewall.

items.title: Every DNS lookup is counted against the router
items.text: The router forwards its clients' lookups. Hand out the resolver's address in the router's DHCP settings. See Record what devices look up.

items.title: Times are hours off
items.text: The container runs in UTC. Set location.timezone, such as Australia/Sydney.

items.title: A notification did not arrive
items.text: The account menu's Notifications page shows the last error under the destination. Send test tries again. Failed messages are not resent.

items.title: An MCP client gets a 404
items.text: Set server.mcp.enabled: true and restart.

items.title: Upgrade notes
items.text: What to change or expect when moving to a release, newest first. Read every section after the release you run, and back up first. A release not listed here needs only the usual steps.

items.title: Breaking changes
items.text:
• config: Group retention, location, server settings (#205)

    a config that sets inventory.retention, auth.* or mcp.enabled, or the matching JOCASTA_ variables, now has those settings ignored. Move them to the new paths.

items.title: Roles
items.text:
Role Can Viewer Read the inventory. Create read tokens. Editor Also edit devices. Create read/write tokens. Admin Also add users and set what each notification destination gets.

The account created on first run is the only admin.

items.title: Add a user
items.text:
1. Open the account menu, top right, and select Users.
  2. Select Add user.
  3. Enter a username (3 to 100 characters), a first password (8 or more), and a role.
  4. Select Create user, and give the person the password.

The web UI cannot change a password or role, remove an account, or reset a forgotten password yet.

items.title: Sessions
items.text:
A sign-in lasts up to 7 days, or 24 hours without use. Without Remember me, it also ends when the browser closes. Set the limits with server.auth.session_lifetime and server.auth.idle_timeout.

After 10 wrong passwords, an account gets one try a minute.

items.title: Two-factor authentication
items.text:
1. Open the account menu and select Security.
  2. Select Turn on two-factor authentication.
  3. Scan the QR code with an authenticator app.
  4. Enter its 6-digit code and select Turn on.
  5. Save the 10 recovery codes. They are shown once. Each one signs you in once without the app.

The same page regenerates the recovery codes or turns two-factor off. Both ask for your password.

items.title: API tokens
items.text:
Scripts and agents use a token to reach the JSON API and the MCP server.

  1. Open the account menu and select API tokens.
  2. Select Create a token.
  3. Name it, and pick Viewer (read) or Editor (read_write) and an expiry. The default never expires.
  4. Select Create token and copy it. It is shown once.

A token can do no more than its account. Revoking it takes effect at once.

items.title: Plugins
items.text:
Plugins read what a sweep cannot reach: routers for devices on every segment and what is plugged in where, flow exports for who talks to whom, and DNS resolvers for what devices look up.

Plugin Devices and networks Topology Traffic DNS lookups MikroTik RouterOS Yes Yes Through NetFlow OpenWrt Yes Yes Through NetFlow NetFlow Yes Technitium Yes Pi-hole Yes AdGuard Home Yes

items.title: Configure a plugin
items.text:
Each plugin is a block under plugins, keyed by kind, then by an instance name you choose:

plugins:
  routeros:
    gateway:                 # instance name, shown as the source
      enabled: true
      host: "192.0.2.1"
      # ...

The instance name is the source its facts are filed under. Router and DNS resolver names share one namespace: a routeros and a technitium instance cannot both be gateway. A netflow listener can share its router's name.

Put passwords in the environment, such as JOCASTA_PLUGINS__ROUTEROS__GATEWAY__PASSWORD; see Configure. Every setting is in the configuration reference.

A source with ssl: false sends its password in the clear, and Jocasta warns at startup.

items.title: Check a plugin
items.text:
jocasta plugin run gateway

reads the source once and prints what it claims. It changes nothing. See CLI.

items.title: Topology
items.text: A MikroTik or OpenWrt router draws the Topology page. Read its switches and access points too for each device's port. See Show what is plugged in where.

items.title: DNS resolvers
items.text: Technitium, Pi-hole and AdGuard Home give each device's lookups. See Record what devices look up.

items.title: AdGuard Home
items.text:
Jocasta reads the query log of an AdGuard Home over its API. What is recorded, and how to route lookups so each device asks AdGuard Home directly, is in Record what devices look up.

plugins:
  adguard:
    resolver:
      enabled: true
      host: "192.0.2.53"
      port: 443
      ssl: true
      user: "jocasta"
      password: "change-me"

Put the web interface login in user and password, or the password in JOCASTA_PLUGINS__ADGUARD__RESOLVER__PASSWORD. AdGuard Home has no read-only users, so the login can change settings too. On a server with no login set, leave user empty.

In AdGuard Home's settings, keep the query log on and client address anonymisation off. An anonymised address names no device, so its lookups count against none.

Each read takes at most 20,000 lookups. If more pile up while Jocasta is stopped, it keeps the newest and logs that it skipped the rest.

items.title: Record what devices look up
items.text:
Jocasta reads the query log of Technitium, Pi-hole v6 or AdGuard Home, and keeps hourly counts of each name each device looked up, blocked or not. With traffic collection on, a device's traffic names each address after the names it looked up.

Technitium Pi-hole AdGuard Home Answer addresses, to name traffic Yes No Yes Read-only login Yes No No

Each resolver is read every minute, up to 20,000 lookups a read. Counts are kept for retention.dns, 30 days by default.

items.title: Point devices at the resolver
items.text: A lookup counts against the address that asked. If the router forwards its clients' lookups, they all count against the router. Hand out the resolver's address as the DNS server in the router's DHCP settings.

items.title: Check it
items.text:
jocasta plugin run resolver

prints the last hour's lookups per device and name.

items.title: NetFlow
items.text:
Jocasta can record which devices talk to which, and to where on the internet, from the flow records your router exports (NetFlow v5, v9 or IPFIX). It keeps hourly totals per device for retention.traffic (30 days by default). Individual connections are not stored.

plugins:
  netflow:
    gateway:
      enabled: true
      listen: ":2055"
      exporters:
        - "192.0.2.1"        # the router's address; anything else is dropped

exporters is required. Only datagrams from the listed addresses are read. A device on the same network can forge that address, so bind listen to an address only the router reaches, or allow the port only from the router in your firewall.

With host networking the listener is reachable as it is. On a bridge network, publish the port as UDP: -p 2055:2055/udp.

items.title: Set up the router
items.text:
Point the router's flow export at the Jocasta host and port:

  • MikroTik RouterOS: Traffic Flow, as IPFIX.
  • OpenWrt: softflowd, as NetFlow v9.

Export from one router only. Two routers that both see a conversation both report it, and it is counted twice.

Internet addresses are shown by the organisation that announces them, and placed on the map by the country they are registered in, using IP to ASN data and IP to Country data by DB-IP, licensed under CC BY 4.0.

The world map draws a line from the network's country to each country it talked to. Jocasta finds its country from the router's outside address. When that address is private, because the ISP puts the router behind carrier-grade NAT, name the country yourself, by its two-letter code. A country named here is used whatever the outside address says:

location:
  country: "AU"

Only the country is used, to start the lines from its middle; nothing finer is asked for or stored.

items.text: Every plugins.netflow setting, with its default and allowed values, is in the configuration reference.

items.title: OpenWrt
items.text:
Jocasta reads OpenWrt over ubus, the JSON-RPC endpoint LuCI uses, at http://<router>/ubus. Any router with LuCI installed serves it, so there is nothing to install. Jocasta reads the neighbour table, the DHCP leases and the static leases, and the interfaces with their VLANs. For the Topology page it also reads the ports, the bridge table and the Wi-Fi clients. It changes nothing on the router.

Give Jocasta a login of its own that can only read. On the router:

  1. Copy openwrt/jocasta.json to /usr/share/rpcd/acl.d/jocasta.json. It grants the reads Jocasta makes and nothing else. LuCI's own groups do not grant the bridge table, so root cannot read it without this file either.
  2. Hash a password for the login:
uhttpd -m 'change-me'
  1. Add the login to /etc/config/rpcd, with the hash the last step printed:
config login
 option username 'jocasta'
 option password '$1$...'
 list read 'jocasta'
  1. Reload rpcd:
/etc/init.d/rpcd reload

Then add the router to Jocasta:

plugins:
  openwrt:
    gateway:                 # instance name, shown as the source
      enabled: true
      host: "192.0.2.1"
      user: "jocasta"
      password: "change-me"  # or JOCASTA_PLUGINS__OPENWRT__GATEWAY__PASSWORD
      ssl: false             # true once luci-ssl is installed
      insecure: false        # true for uhttpd's self-signed cert

Check it with jocasta plugin run gateway. A login rpcd refuses, or one missing the ACL file, reads as credentials rejected.

A name you set under Network → DHCP and DNS → Static Leases ranks above the name a device asks for, as a static lease does on RouterOS. A network is named after its OpenWrt interface, such as lan or iot, and an interface on a VLAN device carries its tag.

items.title: Topology
items.text:
What each OpenWrt table adds to the Topology page:

  • The kernel's bridge table says which port each hardware address is behind. On a router with a DSA switch, as most current ones have, each switch port is a device of its own, so the table names the port. On an older router with a swconfig switch, every switch port is one device, so the table names only that device. rpcd reads at most 256 entries of the table. A bridge that holds more shows the first 256, and the read logs a warning saying so.
  • The bridge-vlan sections of the network configuration say which VLANs each port carries.
  • iwinfo's station list marks Wi-Fi clients and names their network and band, with the rate each way and the signal.
  • LuCI's device list gives the rate each port's link runs at.

OpenWrt runs no neighbour discovery by default, so an OpenWrt source names no neighbours. The router still finds an OpenWrt access point among the addresses on its ports when the access point is read too.

To read an OpenWrt access point for its ports, add it as another instance with topology_only: true. See Show what is plugged in where.

items.title: Export traffic flows
items.text:
To record who devices talk to, install softflowd and point it at the Jocasta host (here 192.0.2.10), then set up the NetFlow listener:

opkg update && opkg install softflowd    # OpenWrt 24.10 and older
apk update && apk add softflowd          # OpenWrt 25.12 and newer
uci set softflowd.@softflowd[0].enabled='1'
uci set softflowd.@softflowd[0].host_port='192.0.2.10:2055'
uci set softflowd.@softflowd[0].export_version='9'
uci set softflowd.@softflowd[0].track_ipv6='1'
uci set softflowd.@softflowd[0].timeout='maxlife=300'
uci delete softflowd.@softflowd[0].sampling_rate
uci commit softflowd
/etc/init.d/softflowd enable
/etc/init.d/softflowd start

Each line changes a default that would cost you traffic:

  • export_version 9 carries IPv6, which the default, 5, cannot. IPFIX (10) works too.
  • track_ipv6 records IPv6 conversations as well as IPv4.
  • maxlife=300 reports a long download every five minutes. Without it, a conversation is reported only when it ends, so a stream that runs all evening lands in the hour it stopped.
  • Deleting sampling_rate counts every packet. The default, 100, counts one in 100. Jocasta scales sampled counts back up, but a conversation of a few packets may not be counted at all.

softflowd watches br-lan, the default LAN bridge. To record another segment, such as a VLAN on br-lan.20, add a softflowd section for its interface, with a pid_file and control_socket of its own. List the router's LAN address in exporters: that is the address the exports come from.

items.title: Pi-hole
items.text:
Jocasta reads the query log of a Pi-hole v6 over its API. What is recorded, and how to route lookups so each device asks Pi-hole directly, is in Record what devices look up. Pi-hole logs no answer addresses, so its lookups name no traffic.

plugins:
  pihole:
    resolver:
      enabled: true
      host: "192.0.2.53"
      port: 443
      ssl: true
      insecure: true         # for Pi-hole's self-signed certificate
      password: "change-me"

To prepare the server:

  1. In Pi-hole's web interface, create an app password.
  2. Put it in password, or in JOCASTA_PLUGINS__PIHOLE__RESOLVER__PASSWORD.

Pi-hole has no read-only login, so the app password can change settings too. Making a new app password signs out every session, Jocasta's included, and Jocasta signs in again on its next read. On a Pi-hole with no password set, leave password empty.

Keep Pi-hole's privacy level at the one that shows everything. A level that hides domains or clients hides them from Jocasta too.

Each read takes at most 20,000 lookups. If more pile up while Jocasta is stopped, it keeps the newest and logs that it skipped the rest.

items.text: Every plugins.pihole setting, with its default and allowed values, is in the configuration reference.

items.title: MikroTik RouterOS
items.text:
Jocasta reads RouterOS over its REST API:

plugins:
  routeros:
    gateway:                 # instance name, shown as the source
      enabled: true
      host: "192.0.2.1"
      user: "jocasta"        # a read-only user is enough
      password: "change-me"  # or JOCASTA_PLUGINS__ROUTEROS__GATEWAY__PASSWORD
      ssl: true
      insecure: true         # RouterOS serves a self-signed cert unless you import one

Check it with jocasta plugin run gateway before starting the server. See CLI.

items.title: Topology
items.text:
What each RouterOS table adds to the Topology page:

  • The bridge host table says which port each hardware address is behind, and in which VLAN when the bridge has VLAN filtering on.
  • Neighbour discovery (MNDP or LLDP) names the switch or access point on each port. RouterOS runs it on the LAN interface list by default; see /ip neighbor discovery-settings.
  • The Wi-Fi registration table marks Wi-Fi clients and names their network and band, from the wifi or the wireless package, with the rate each way and the signal. A router managing access points with CAPsMAN lists their clients too.
  • The Ethernet monitor gives the rate each Ethernet and SFP port's link runs at, and the fastest rate both ends offer.

To read a MikroTik switch or access point for its ports, add it as another instance with topology_only: true. See Show what is plugged in where.

items.title: Export traffic flows
items.text:
To record who devices talk to, point Traffic Flow at the Jocasta host (here 192.0.2.10) and set up the NetFlow listener:

/ip traffic-flow set enabled=yes interfaces=all
/ip traffic-flow target add dst-address=192.0.2.10 port=2055 version=ipfix

items.title: All settings
items.text: Every plugins.routeros setting, with its default and allowed values, is in the configuration reference.

items.title: Technitium
items.text:
Jocasta reads the query log of a Technitium DNS Server over its HTTP API. What is recorded, and how to route lookups so each device asks the server directly, is in Record what devices look up.

plugins:
  technitium:
    resolver:
      enabled: true
      host: "192.0.2.53"
      port: 53443
      ssl: true
      insecure: true         # for the server's self-signed certificate
      token: "change-me"

To prepare the server:

  1. In Apps, App Store, install Query Logs (Sqlite). Technitium keeps a query log only through an app like this one.
  2. In Administration, Users, add a user for Jocasta. In Administration, Permissions, give that user View on the Logs section and nothing else.
  3. Sign in as that user, and in the user menu select Create API Token. Put the token in token, or in JOCASTA_PLUGINS__TECHNITIUM__RESOLVER__TOKEN.

With more than one app logging queries, name the one to read in log_app, as the Apps page lists it.

In a cluster, each node logs the lookups it answered to its own disk. Add one entry per node, each at that node's own address. A virtual address shared between nodes, such as one VRRP keeps, reaches one node at a time, and the other node's lookups would go unread. The token and the log app reach every node from the primary.

items.title: All settings
items.text: Every plugins.technitium setting, with its default and allowed values, is in the configuration reference.

items.title: Show what is plugged in where
items.text:
The Topology page draws the network from the internet down: router, switches, access points, and each device on its port or Wi-Fi network. It comes from the bridge and Wi-Fi tables of each MikroTik and OpenWrt router Jocasta reads. A switch or access point that announces itself to the router shows up with the devices behind it.

To see which switch port each device is on, read the switch too, with topology_only: true:

plugins:
  routeros:
    gateway:
      enabled: true
      host: "192.0.2.1"
      # ...
    switch_core:
      enabled: true
      host: "192.0.2.2"
      user: "jocasta"
      password: "change-me"
      topology_only: true    # ports only; the router lists the devices

A topology_only source finds no devices, so its management address cannot rename a network. Every RouterOS and OpenWrt source is read on scan.devices.interval.

jocasta plugin run switch_core prints its ports, the addresses on each, and its neighbours.

What each router's tables add: RouterOS, OpenWrt. How to read the page: Tour the web UI.
